subtopic_detail: recognising anterior pituitary failure when lactation never establishes after a major obstetric haemorrhage
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 32 year old woman ten weeks after the birth of her second child. Her delivery was complicated by a postpartum haemorrhage of 3 200 mL requiring six units of red cells and a period of hypotension in the operating theatre.

She tells you she was never able to produce enough milk despite persistent effort with a lactation consultant, and gave up at four weeks. She has had no periods since the birth, feels exhausted, is cold all the time and has become dizzy on standing. She has no headache and no visual disturbance. She is not breastfeeding now and a pregnancy test is negative. Her thyroid stimulating hormone is 0.8 mIU/L with a free thyroxine of 7 pmol/L, her 9 am cortisol is 62 nmol/L, and her prolactin is below the detection limit of the assay.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 92/min, blood pressure 96/60 mmHg lying and 82/54 mmHg standing, respiratory rate 16/min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.2 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Pallor with dry skin, loss of axillary and pubic hair, no goitre, visual fields full to confrontation, no galactorrhoea, breasts soft and non engorged
data_table.Investigations: Thyroid stimulating hormone 0.8 mIU/L (0.4-4.0) with free thyroxine 7 pmol/L (10-20), 9 am cortisol 62 nmol/L (200-700), prolactin undetectable, sodium 129 mmol/L (135-145), potassium 4.2 mmol/L (3.5-5.2), beta human chorionic gonadotrophin negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Replace hydrocortisone first, then thyroxine, and image the pituitary
options.rationale: A low free thyroxine with an inappropriately normal thyroid stimulating hormone, an undetectable prolactin and a low 9 am cortisol together indicate panhypopituitarism, which in this context follows ischaemic necrosis of the pituitary after major obstetric haemorrhage. The order matters critically, because thyroxine accelerates cortisol clearance and giving it before glucocorticoid replacement can precipitate an adrenal crisis, and imaging then confirms the empty or shrunken gland. (Source: Endocrine Society of Australia)

options.text: Start levothyroxine now and review her thyroid function again in six weeks
options.rationale: Thyroxine replacement is indeed needed, and starting it before glucocorticoid in a patient with unrecognised adrenal insufficiency increases metabolic demand and cortisol clearance and can precipitate a life threatening crisis. The sequence rather than the drug is the error. (Source: Endocrine Society of Australia)

options.text: Reassure her that amenorrhoea and fatigue are expected in the postnatal period
options.rationale: Postnatal fatigue and lactational amenorrhoea are extremely common and would be the right interpretation in a woman who is breastfeeding and otherwise well. Failure of lactation, postural hypotension, hyponatraemia and loss of secondary sexual hair are not features of normal recovery. (Source: Endocrine Society of Australia)

options.text: Commence the combined oral contraceptive pill to restore her menstrual cycle
options.rationale: Oestrogen replacement is part of long term management of the gonadotrophin deficiency and addresses only one of several failing axes. Prescribing it alone would produce withdrawal bleeds while leaving untreated the cortisol and thyroxine deficiencies that are making her unwell and putting her at risk. (Source: Endocrine Society of Australia)

options.text: Measure thyroid autoantibodies and treat this as postpartum thyroiditis instead
options.rationale: Postpartum thyroiditis is common and causes a hypothyroid phase within the first year, and it produces a raised thyroid stimulating hormone because the pituitary responds normally to a failing thyroid. Her thyroid stimulating hormone is inappropriately normal with a low free thyroxine, which localises the problem to the pituitary. (Source: Endocrine Society of Australia)

explanation.summary: Sheehan syndrome is infarction of the anterior pituitary caused by hypotension from major obstetric haemorrhage, occurring because the gland enlarges during pregnancy and outgrows its low pressure portal blood supply. The earliest and most characteristic clinical clue is failure of lactation, since prolactin secreting cells are affected, followed by amenorrhoea, fatigue, cold intolerance and loss of axillary and pubic hair. The biochemical signature is deficiency across several axes with inappropriately low or normal trophic hormones, and the key interpretive point is that a low free thyroxine with a normal thyroid stimulating hormone is a pituitary result rather than a normal one. Hyponatraemia from glucocorticoid deficiency is common. Hydrocortisone must be replaced before thyroxine, because thyroid hormone increases cortisol clearance and metabolic demand and can precipitate an adrenal crisis in an unreplaced patient.
key_points: Failure of lactation after major obstetric haemorrhage is the earliest clue to pituitary infarction.
A low free thyroxine with a normal thyroid stimulating hormone indicates pituitary rather than thyroid failure.
An undetectable prolactin in the postnatal period is strongly abnormal and supports the diagnosis.
Hyponatraemia with normal potassium reflects glucocorticoid deficiency with preserved mineralocorticoid function.
Glucocorticoid must always be replaced before thyroxine to avoid precipitating an adrenal crisis.
explanation.pearls: Always give hydrocortisone before levothyroxine when replacing multiple pituitary hormones, because thyroxine accelerates cortisol clearance and raises metabolic demand, and starting it first in an unreplaced patient can precipitate a fatal adrenal crisis within days.

subtopic_detail: responding to a thickened plaque arising within long standing white atrophic vulval skin
stem:
You are the gynaecologist reviewing a 64 year old woman who has had vulval itching for nine years, diagnosed as lichen sclerosus on biopsy six years ago and controlled with an ultrapotent topical corticosteroid used intermittently.

She has attended today because one area now feels different. Over the past four months a firm raised area has developed on the right labium majus, and it has not changed despite eight weeks of daily ultrapotent topical corticosteroid, which had always settled her symptoms before. She has no vaginal bleeding and no discharge. Her cervical screening history is complete and normal, and she has never smoked. On examination the vulval skin is generally pale, thinned and crinkled with loss of the labia minora and narrowing of the introitus, and within that skin there is a 15 mm firm indurated plaque on the right labium majus.

data_table.Examination: Generalised vulval pallor with thinned crinkled skin, resorption of the labia minora, introital narrowing, a discrete 15 mm firm indurated plaque on the right labium majus with an intact surface, no inguinal lymphadenopathy
data_table.Investigations: Vulval swab negative for candida and bacterial pathogens, previous vulval biopsy six years ago confirmed lichen sclerosus

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Escalate to a topical calcineurin inhibitor applied twice daily for three months
options.rationale: Tacrolimus and pimecrolimus are second line agents for lichen sclerosus that has not responded to corticosteroid, and using one here would treat a lesion that has not been characterised. Three months of a further topical agent delays the histological answer that a non responding indurated area demands. (Source: RANZCOG: Vulval disorders)

options.text: Biopsy the thickened area to exclude vulval intraepithelial neoplasia
options.rationale: Lichen sclerosus carries a lifetime risk of vulval squamous cell carcinoma of around four to five percent, and the transition is heralded by exactly this change: a localised area that becomes thickened, indurated, ulcerated or fails to respond to treatment that previously worked. Biopsy of the specific abnormal area, rather than of unaffected skin, is the only way to distinguish differentiated vulval intraepithelial neoplasia or an early carcinoma from hypertrophic lichen sclerosus. (Source: RANZCOG: Vulval disorders)

options.text: Reassure her that this represents hypertrophic disease and review in six months
options.rationale: Hypertrophic or thickened plaques do occur within lichen sclerosus and cannot be distinguished clinically from differentiated vulval intraepithelial neoplasia or early invasion, which is why they are biopsied rather than observed. Six months of review would allow an early carcinoma to progress to nodal disease. (Source: RANZCOG: Vulval disorders)

options.text: Arrange magnetic resonance imaging of the pelvis and groins before any biopsy
options.rationale: Cross sectional imaging stages disease once malignancy has been confirmed histologically and defines nodal involvement before surgery. Performed before any tissue diagnosis it cannot distinguish a benign plaque from a malignant one, because that distinction is cellular rather than anatomical. (Source: RANZCOG: Vulval disorders)

options.text: Refer for wide local excision of the entire affected vulval skin without biopsy
options.rationale: Wide excision is the treatment for confirmed neoplasia and its extent is determined by the histology and margins required, so operating before diagnosis risks both inadequate and unnecessarily mutilating surgery. Excising all lichen sclerosus affected skin would also be disfiguring and would not prevent recurrence elsewhere. (Source: RANZCOG: Vulval disorders)

explanation.summary: Lichen sclerosus is a chronic inflammatory dermatosis producing pallor, thinning and crinkling of vulval skin with architectural loss including resorption of the labia minora and introital narrowing. It is controlled rather than cured with ultrapotent topical corticosteroid, and long term maintenance treatment reduces both symptoms and the risk of malignant transformation. The lifetime risk of vulval squamous cell carcinoma is around four to five percent, and malignancy characteristically arises through differentiated vulval intraepithelial neoplasia, which is not associated with human papillomavirus and occurs in older women on a background of lichen sclerosus. The warning signs are a localised thickened, indurated, ulcerated or eroded area, or failure to respond to previously effective treatment. Any such area requires biopsy of the abnormal site rather than escalation of topical therapy or clinical observation.
key_points: Lichen sclerosus causes pallor, thinning, crinkling and architectural loss with introital narrowing.
Lifetime risk of vulval squamous cell carcinoma is about four to five percent.
Differentiated vulval intraepithelial neoplasia arises on lichen sclerosus and is not related to human papillomavirus.
Induration, ulceration or failure to respond to previously effective corticosteroid mandates biopsy.
Long term maintenance topical corticosteroid reduces symptoms, architectural damage and cancer risk.
explanation.pearls: Biopsy any area of lichen sclerosus that stops responding to a corticosteroid that previously worked, because differentiated vulval intraepithelial neoplasia cannot be distinguished clinically from a hypertrophic plaque and is the route by which around one in twenty of these women develop squamous cell carcinoma.

subtopic_detail: deciding whether to attempt instrumental birth in the room or move to theatre when the head is not as low as the caput suggests
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar called to a birth suite for a 28 year old woman in her first pregnancy at 40 weeks. She has been pushing for two hours with an epidural in place and is becoming exhausted.

The cardiotocograph shows a baseline of 150 beats per minute with variable decelerations to 90 recovering within a minute, and normal variability. On abdominal palpation two fifths of the head is palpable above the pubic symphysis. On vaginal examination the cervix is fully dilated, the head is in the right occipitotransverse position, there is 3 plus caput and 2 plus moulding, and the presenting part feels to be at the level of the ischial spines. The liquor is clear. The birth suite is adjacent to the operating theatre and an anaesthetist is present in the unit.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 96/min, blood pressure 118/74 mmHg, respiratory rate 18/min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 37.0 degrees C, foetal heart rate 150/min
data_table.Examination: Two fifths of the head palpable abdominally, cervix fully dilated, right occipitotransverse position, station at the ischial spines, caput 3 plus, moulding 2 plus, clear liquor, effective epidural in place
data_table.Investigations: Cardiotocograph baseline 150/min with normal variability and variable decelerations to 90/min recovering within one minute

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Apply non rotational forceps in the room and deliver in the current position
options.rationale: Non rotational forceps require an occipitoanterior position, and applying them to a head in the transverse position would be a misapplication with a high risk of facial nerve injury and severe maternal trauma. The position alone excludes this instrument. (Source: RANZCOG: Instrumental vaginal birth)

options.text: Continue pushing for a further hour with oxytocin augmentation commenced
options.rationale: Augmentation with more time is reasonable for inadequate contractions with a well applied head making gradual progress, and this woman has already pushed for two hours with significant caput and moulding indicating obstruction. Adding another hour increases the risks of obstructed labour without addressing why the head has not descended. (Source: RANZCOG: Instrumental vaginal birth)

options.text: Move to theatre for a trial of instrumental birth with immediate recourse to caesarean
options.rationale: Two fifths of the head palpable abdominally means that engagement is marginal and the station felt vaginally is being exaggerated by 3 plus caput and 2 plus moulding, which makes this a mid cavity birth with a transverse position and a genuine chance of failure. Conducting the attempt in theatre with the team assembled allows immediate progression to caesarean section if the instrument does not deliver, which is the arrangement that avoids a delayed second attempt with a deeply impacted head. (Source: RANZCOG: Instrumental vaginal birth)

options.text: Perform an immediate category one caesarean section without any vaginal attempt
options.rationale: A category one caesarean is for immediate threat to maternal or foetal life, and this cardiotocograph has normal variability with variable decelerations that recover within a minute, which does not meet that threshold. Committing straight to caesarean at full dilatation with the head at the spines also carries a real risk of a difficult impacted head. (Source: RANZCOG: Instrumental vaginal birth)

options.text: Attempt manual rotation and vacuum extraction in the room with paediatric support
options.rationale: Manual rotation followed by vacuum is a recognised technique for a transverse position and is appropriate when the head is well engaged with minimal caput and moulding. With two fifths palpable abdominally and marked caput, doing it in the room removes the immediate recourse to caesarean that this degree of uncertainty demands. (Source: RANZCOG: Instrumental vaginal birth)

explanation.summary: The critical skill in this scenario is recognising that caput and moulding make the vaginal station misleading, so abdominal palpation is the more reliable guide to descent. Two fifths of the head palpable abdominally with 3 plus caput and 2 plus moulding means the true station is higher than the spines suggests, placing this in mid cavity territory with an occipitotransverse position. Instrumental birth in these circumstances has a meaningfully higher failure rate, which is why the attempt belongs in theatre as a trial with the team prepared to proceed immediately to caesarean section. Non rotational forceps are excluded by the transverse position. The cardiotocograph does not meet category one criteria, so there is time to move the woman and prepare properly.
key_points: Caput and moulding falsely lower the apparent station, so abdominal palpation is the more reliable measure of descent.
More than one fifth of the head palpable abdominally makes instrumental birth substantially more likely to fail.
Non rotational forceps require an occipitoanterior position and are contraindicated in a transverse position.
A trial of instrumental birth in theatre allows immediate recourse to caesarean section without a second attempt.
Category one caesarean requires immediate threat to life, which normal variability with recovering variables does not meet.
explanation.pearls: Palpate the abdomen before every instrumental birth and treat more than one fifth palpable with 3 plus caput as a trial in theatre rather than a birth in the room, because caput and moulding routinely make a mid cavity head feel as though it is at the spines.

subtopic_detail: selecting bone protection in a recently menopausal woman with troublesome flushes and an intact uterus
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 53 year old woman whose last menstrual period was two years ago. She has twelve to fifteen hot flushes a day and wakes drenched most nights, and she has stopped attending her book club because of them.

Her mother fractured a hip at 70. She is a lifelong non smoker, drinks two standard drinks a week and walks daily. She has an intact uterus, has never had a venous thrombosis, has no personal or family history of breast cancer and her mammogram last month was normal. Her blood pressure is 118/74 mmHg and her body mass index is 24 kg/m2. A bone mineral density scan performed because of her family history shows a lumbar spine T score of minus 2.1 and a femoral neck T score of minus 1.9, and she has had no fractures. Her calcium, vitamin D and thyroid function are all normal.

data_table.Examination: Body mass index 24 kg/m2, blood pressure 118/74 mmHg, no breast masses, no spinal tenderness, height unchanged from her recorded height at age 40
data_table.Investigations: Lumbar spine T score minus 2.1, femoral neck T score minus 1.9, corrected calcium 2.35 mmol/L (2.10-2.60), 25 hydroxyvitamin D 78 nmol/L (50-150), thyroid stimulating hormone 2.1 mIU/L (0.4-4.0), mammogram normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first line treatment?

options.text: Oral alendronate weekly with calcium and vitamin D supplementation added
options.rationale: A bisphosphonate is first line for established osteoporosis defined by a T score at or below minus 2.5 or a minimal trauma fracture, neither of which she has. It also does nothing for the vasomotor symptoms that are her presenting problem and are the reason she has withdrawn from her activities. (Source: Australasian Menopause Society)

options.text: Combined oestrogen and progestogen menopausal hormone therapy
options.rationale: She is within ten years of her final menstrual period and under 60, the window in which the balance of benefit and risk for hormone therapy is most favourable, and it is the most effective treatment for vasomotor symptoms while also preventing the accelerated bone loss of the early postmenopausal years. A progestogen must accompany the oestrogen because she has an intact uterus and unopposed oestrogen causes endometrial hyperplasia and carcinoma. (Source: Australasian Menopause Society)

options.text: Transdermal oestradiol used alone without any additional endometrial protection
options.rationale: The transdermal route is a sound choice and carries a lower venous thromboembolism risk than oral oestrogen, so the delivery method here is not the error. Giving oestrogen without a progestogen to a woman with an intact uterus is the error, because unopposed oestrogen drives endometrial hyperplasia and carcinoma. (Source: Australasian Menopause Society)

options.text: Denosumab by subcutaneous injection every six months with calcium monitoring
options.rationale: Denosumab is a potent antiresorptive used in established osteoporosis, often where bisphosphonates are unsuitable, and it requires uninterrupted six monthly dosing because cessation causes rapid rebound bone loss with vertebral fractures. Committing a 53 year old with osteopenia to that long term obligation is disproportionate. (Source: Royal Australian College of General Practitioners: Osteoporosis)
source_refs: Royal Australian College of General Practitioners: Osteoporosis

options.text: Venlafaxine at a low dose with weight bearing exercise and dietary calcium advice
options.rationale: A serotonin and noradrenaline reuptake inhibitor is a reasonable non hormonal option for flushes in women who cannot take or decline hormone therapy, and it is less effective than oestrogen and offers no skeletal benefit. She has no contraindication to hormone therapy, so accepting a weaker option for both of her problems is not justified. (Source: Australasian Menopause Society)

explanation.summary: This woman has two problems that one treatment addresses: troublesome vasomotor symptoms and osteopenia with a family history of hip fracture. Menopausal hormone therapy is the most effective treatment for vasomotor symptoms and also prevents the rapid bone loss of the early postmenopausal years, which makes it the rational first choice. The timing hypothesis matters, since initiation under 60 years or within ten years of the final menstrual period carries a favourable balance of benefit and risk, whereas starting much later increases cardiovascular risk. A progestogen is mandatory alongside oestrogen in any woman with an intact uterus to prevent endometrial hyperplasia and carcinoma. Bisphosphonates and denosumab are reserved for established osteoporosis rather than osteopenia in a symptomatic woman of this age.
key_points: Hormone therapy is the most effective treatment for vasomotor symptoms and also preserves bone density.
The favourable window is initiation under 60 years or within ten years of the final menstrual period.
A progestogen is mandatory with systemic oestrogen in any woman who has an intact uterus.
Osteoporosis is defined by a T score at or below minus 2.5 or by a minimal trauma fracture.
Transdermal oestrogen carries a lower venous thromboembolism risk than the oral route.
explanation.pearls: Treat osteopenia in a symptomatic woman within ten years of her last period with menopausal hormone therapy rather than a bisphosphonate, because it addresses the flushes and the bone loss together, and never prescribe systemic oestrogen without a progestogen when the uterus is intact.

sources.label: Royal Australian College of General Practitioners: Osteoporosis

subtopic_detail: advising parents about episodes of screaming early in the night that the child cannot recall next morning
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing the parents of a 4 year old boy who have come without him because they are frightened by what happens at night.

They describe that about ninety minutes after he falls asleep he sits up and screams, his eyes are open but he does not seem to see them, he is sweaty with a racing heart, and he pushes them away when they try to comfort him. It lasts around five minutes and then he lies down and sleeps. In the morning he is cheerful and has no memory of it at all. It happens two or three times a week and always in the first part of the night. He started four year old kindergarten six weeks ago and has been going to bed later than usual. He is developing normally, has no daytime symptoms and there is no snoring.

data_table.Examination: Well grown and developmentally appropriate on parental report, no dysmorphic features described, tonsils not enlarged on a recent review, no daytime behavioural concerns reported by kindergarten

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Prescribe a low dose benzodiazepine at night for the next three months
options.rationale: Benzodiazepines suppress slow wave sleep and are occasionally used for frequent, dangerous or highly disruptive parasomnias in older children after other measures have failed. They are disproportionate for a benign self limiting phenomenon in a preschooler and carry sedation and behavioural risks. (Source: Sleep Health Foundation: Sleep terrors)

options.text: Refer for overnight polysomnography to characterise the nocturnal episodes
options.rationale: Sleep studies are indicated when the history is atypical, when episodes are stereotyped and very frequent suggesting nocturnal seizures, or when obstructive sleep apnoea is suspected as a trigger. This history is entirely typical and there is no snoring or daytime sleepiness. (Source: Sleep Health Foundation: Sleep terrors)

options.text: Advise the parents to wake him fully during each episode and comfort him
options.rationale: Attempting to rouse a child during one of these episodes typically prolongs it and increases agitation and confusion, because he is in deep sleep rather than awake and frightened. The advice is to stay nearby and keep him safe without waking him. (Source: Sleep Health Foundation: Sleep terrors)

options.text: Start an antidepressant to reduce the anxiety underlying the night time distress
options.rationale: Medication for anxiety would be considered where a child had daytime anxiety symptoms or nightmares related to a specific stressor or trauma. He has no daytime symptoms, and the episodes occur in deep sleep rather than arising from dream content. (Source: Sleep Health Foundation: Sleep terrors)

options.text: Reassure the parents, advise on safety, and address his sleep schedule
options.rationale: These episodes arise from incomplete arousal out of slow wave sleep, which is concentrated in the first third of the night, and they resolve spontaneously as the child matures without any treatment. The practical advice is to keep the environment safe, avoid waking him, and correct the sleep deprivation caused by his later bedtime, since insufficient sleep increases slow wave sleep pressure and directly increases episode frequency. (Source: Sleep Health Foundation: Sleep terrors)

explanation.summary: Sleep terrors are a disorder of arousal from slow wave sleep and are common in preschool and early school aged children. The features that identify them are timing in the first third of the night, autonomic arousal with sweating and tachycardia, apparent unresponsiveness to comforting, and complete amnesia for the event the following morning. Nightmares are the main differential and differ on every one of those points, occurring in the second half of the night during rapid eye movement sleep, with the child fully awakened, consolable and able to describe the dream. Management is reassurance, safety measures such as securing stairs and windows, and attention to sleep deprivation, which is the commonest precipitant because it increases slow wave sleep rebound. Investigation and medication are reserved for atypical, injurious or very frequent episodes.
key_points: Sleep terrors arise from slow wave sleep and occur in the first third of the night.
Complete amnesia for the episode the next morning is characteristic and distinguishes them from nightmares.
Nightmares occur in the second half of the night with full waking, consolability and dream recall.
Sleep deprivation increases slow wave sleep pressure and is the commonest precipitant.
Attempting to wake the child during an episode prolongs and worsens it.
explanation.pearls: Ask whether the child remembers the episode in the morning, because complete amnesia with timing early in the night identifies a sleep terror needing only reassurance and an earlier bedtime, whereas vivid recall late in the night points to nightmares and a different conversation entirely.
